title: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Multi-Party Collaborative Dialogues
shows: A benchmark of multi-party, million-token team conversations where current memory systems fail on multi-hop questions and on time reasoning without explicit version information.
takeaway: Store version and supersession data on every fact, and test the brain on multi-person team threads, not only one-on-one chat.

title: Locomo-Plus: Beyond-Factual Cognitive Memory Evaluation Framework for LLM Agents
shows: Finds that older memory benchmarks mostly test explicit fact recall, and that remembering unstated goals or constraints is much harder for current memory systems.
takeaway: Do not judge the brain only on fact lookup; add tests for constraints and preferences that a query does not mention directly.

title: A Simple Yet Strong Baseline for Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
shows: Splits each chat session into standalone, entity-normalized statements linked in a graph, matching strong baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval_S with much shorter answer contexts.
takeaway: Index small entity-normalized statements that point back to the source message, rather than whole transcripts or lossy summaries.

title: SWE-chat: Coding Agent Interactions From Real Users in the Wild
shows: A dataset of nearly 18,000 real coding-agent sessions showing only 59% of agent code survives into commits and users push back in about half of turns.
takeaway: Session logs carry strong signals such as pushback and rework; mine those as pointers to lessons instead of treating every turn as knowledge.

title: CODESKILL: Learning Self-Evolving Skills for Coding Agents
shows: Trains a model to extract reusable skills from coding-agent trajectories and prune the skill bank, improving success on three coding benchmarks over a no-skill baseline.
takeaway: Extraction from agent sessions can pay off, but keep the skill bank small and score each skill by outcome before sharing it company-wide.

title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
shows: Stores single skills plus reusable skill compositions from successful runs, and picks between them with a graph selector that accounts for dependencies.
takeaway: Link skills to their prerequisites and to the sessions they came from, so a retrieved skill arrives with its context.

title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
shows: Six memory systems completed at most 1.5% of forget requests end to end, leaving data extractable or deleting far more than asked.
takeaway: Do not trust a memory layer's delete call; build deletion as a tested workflow and probe for the data afterward.

title: Forgetting Without Restarting: Execution-State Unlearning for Stateful LLM Agents
shows: Deleting a memory record leaves summaries, plans and caches that still carry the data; replaying only the affected part matched a full reset at up to 9x fewer tokens.
takeaway: Record which derived items came from each source so a deletion can find and rebuild every dependent summary, not just the original pointer.

title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
shows: A single query often recovers a deleted secret from derived data like summaries, while provenance-aware controls removed the observed recovery and a literal write filter did not.
takeaway: Track provenance for every derived record and run a post-deletion audit query as part of each right-to-be-forgotten request.

title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
shows: Forgetting inside model weights is not enough, because stored memory or tool calls can bring the data back; current methods leave a gap at the whole-agent level.
takeaway: A deleted fact can return through a live fetch from the source app, so deletion must also be honored at the source and in cached results.

title: Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible in HNSW Vector Databases
shows: Soft-deleted vectors stay in HNSW index files and can be inverted to recover personal details; encrypting vectors and discarding the key on delete removed the observed recovery.
takeaway: A tombstone flag is not erasure; encrypt index entries per record or per epoch so deletion can be proven by destroying a key.

title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
shows: Argues that retrieval-time fixes are not enough and proposes governance built on storage-time provenance, versioning and retention policies.
takeaway: Set provenance, versioning and a retention rule when an entry is written, since they are hard to add after the fact.

title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline
shows: Across six datasets no single matching method wins, precision and recall need different fixes, and one wrong link can chain many unrelated records together.
takeaway: Keep identity links reversible and re-check any merge across groups, because one bad person or project merge can contaminate many pointers.

title: LLM-Powered Knowledge Graphs for Enterprise Intelligence and Analytics
shows: Proposes an LLM framework that merges emails, calendars, chats, documents and logs into one activity-centered graph, and reports gains in expertise finding and task management.
takeaway: An activity graph across apps is a plausible route to expertise finding; treat the reported gains as unproven until tested on our own data.

title: A Qualitative Study of User Perception of M365 AI Copilot
shows: Interviews with 27 people after a six-month trial found value in retrieval and summaries, but concerns about privacy, transparency and bias, and a need for human review.
takeaway: Show users where each answer came from and what the brain can see; transparency is a trust feature, not decoration.

title: Generative AI in Knowledge Work: Perception, Usefulness, and Acceptance of Microsoft 365 Copilot
shows: Repeated employee surveys at a research organization found most value in structured, text-based tasks, with staff groups rating usefulness differently over time.
takeaway: Pilot with different roles separately and re-measure over months, since early opinions shift with use.
